Drugs & Therapies.content:
Some types of pain don’t respond to currently available medicines. Ambros Therapeutics’ in-licensed drug candidate is in pivotal testing for a particular rare type of pain with no FDA-approved therapies, and the biotech will continue developing that program as a public company by merging with Nasdaq-listed Werewolf Therapeutics.
The combined company will keep the Ambros name and operate from that company’s headquarters in San Diego. Along with the all-stock business combination announced Friday, Ambros will be supported by a $150 million private placement expected to support the biotech’s lead molecule up to an FDA submission. The combined company will be led by current Ambros CEO Joseph “Jay” Hagan, who was most recently the chief executive of
Regulus Therapeutics, a developer of microRNA-targeting drugs that was acquired by Novartis
last year.
Ambros’s lead indication is complex regional pain syndrome type 1 (CRPS-1), a rare disorder in which intense limb pain follows an injury or trauma, such as a bone fracture or surgery. This pain typically presents in phases, the company said in an
investor presentation
. In the “warm” phase, patients experience redness, swelling, pain, and a feeling of warmth in the six to 12 months following the initial injury. That period is followed by a “cold” phase characterized by severe and persistent pain, vasoconstriction, and discoloration that makes the affected limb look pale or blue. CRPS has two types; type 2 has more involvement of nerve pain. Currently available pain drugs, including opioids, offer limited efficacy for CRPS.
Sponsored Post
Where Will AI Deployment Benefit Payers the Most?
We are taking a look at how health insurers are using AI, defining success, and managing cybersecurity risks. Give us your opinions by completing our brief, anonymous survey.
By MedCity News
Ambros’s small molecule, neridronate, belongs to a class of medicines called bisphonates, therapies that treat osteoporosis by preventing bone loss. The company describes neridronate as a differentiated bisphonate. As an intravenously infused drug, more of the main pharmaceutical ingredient is available to offer a therapeutic effect compared to bisphonates formulated as pills, which have more limited bioavailability. Neridronate was initially developed by Italy-based Abiogen Pharma, which steered the drug to approval in its home country in 2016 and sells the product there under the brand name Nerixia. Ambros licensed North American rights to neridronate and holds an option for broader market expansion of the molecule.
In the investor presentation, Ambros said neridronate works by concentrating at the site of the injury during the warm phase. There, the drug reduces bone loss and inflammation. Results from the pivotal studies that supported neridronate’s approval in Italy showed greater than 50% reduction in pain scores and reduced pain intensity compared to a placebo. The drug was well tolerated in clinical testing as well as the commercial setting, where it has been used by more than 600,000 patients.
Ambros aims to succeed where Grünenthal fell short. The German pharmaceutical company licensed rights to neridronate in 2013, but ended up returning them after stopping two Phase 3 studies for futility. In the investor presentation, Ambros said Grünenthal’s studies enrolled CPRS type 1 and type 2 patients with no nuclear imaging to assess bone involvement. Also, most participants were advanced past the warm stage. But there was encouraging data in patients with CRPS-1 who were in the warm stage at baseline.
Ambros’s Phase 3 test is expected to enroll 270 adults with the warm subtype of CRPS-1; preliminary data are expected in 2028. The company said it the FDA has agreed a single Phase 3 trial would be sufficient to support regulatory approval. If the trial readout is positive, Ambros said it could file a new drug application in 2029.
presented by
Sponsored Post
The Healthcare Payments Industry Faces a Perception Challenge
Healthcare payments are no longer about transactions. It’s about controlling the revenue cycle. And increasingly, that control is not sitting with ISOs.
By Lisa Brooks, Vice President, Healthcare Partnerships
Going forward, Ambros will focus on neridronate, shelving the cancer assets of
Werewolf, which joined the public markets in 2021
. The biotech’s cytokine therapies are made with technology that keeps a drug “masked” as it circulates throughout the body, activating the therapy only upon reaching tumors. While the two lead programs yielded encouraging early clinical data, Werewolf’s dwindling cash last year highlighted the urgency of finding a big pharmaceutical partner to continue development of its pipeline. No deals were struck. In February of this year, Werewolf restructured operations and started exploring strategic alternatives for the business.
Ambros launched
last December, backed by $125 million in Series A financing led by RA Capital Management and Enavate Sciences. RA Capital will co-lead the private placement with Janus Henderson Investors. Other disclosed investors in this financing include Aberdeen Investments, Adage Capital Partners, ADAR1 Capital Management, Affinity Asset Advisors, Arkin Bio Capital, Balyasny Asset Management, Enavate Sciences, SilverArc Capital, Sphera Healthcare, and Woodline Partners.
The private placement will close concurrent with the close of the business combination, which is expected by the first quarter of 2027. Ambros estimates the proceeds from the deal will last into the first half of 2029. Shareholders of both Ambros and Werewolf still need to approve the merger, which values Ambros at about $500 million. Upon the deal’s close, pre-merger Ambros stockholders will own about 71.7% of the combined company while investors in the private placement hold a 21.5% stake. Pre-merger Werewolf shareholders will own about 6.8% of the combined company. The newly public Ambros is expected to trade on the Nasdaq under the stick symbol “AMBX.”

Werewolf Therapeutics Strikes Reverse Merger With Ambros, Secures $150 Million for Rare Pain Drug
Add to Google Preferred Sources
Werewolf Therapeutics and Ambros Therapeutics agreed to an all-stock reverse merger, with the combined company operating as Ambros and trading on Nasdaq under ticker AMBX. The deal includes a $150 million private placement co-led by RA Capital Management and Janus Henderson Investors, extending the cash runway into the first half of 2029. Werewolf shareholders will own about 6.8% of the combined entity, while Ambros stockholders hold approximately 71.7%. Ambros is developing neridronate for complex regional pain syndrome type 1, a chronic pain condition affecting 50,000 to 70,000 new U.S. patients annually with no FDA-approved treatments. The drug, already approved in Italy, has Breakthrough Therapy, Fast Track, and Orphan Drug designations. A Phase 3 trial is expected to report results in 2028, with a potential FDA filing to follow. Werewolf shares surged more than 127% in premarket trading on the announcement.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration
Nasdaq
Werewolf Therapeutics Inc. (HOWL) has found an exit from its strategic review, agreeing Friday to a reverse merger with privately held Ambros Therapeutics Inc. in an all-stock transaction that will hand control of the Nasdaq listing to a company developing a treatment for a debilitating pain condition.
The combined company will operate under the Ambros name and trade on Nasdaq under the ticker AMBX, with a concurrent $150 million private placement co-led by RA Capital Management and Janus Henderson Investors. Ambros expects the financing to carry operations through pivotal Phase 3 results in 2028, a planned new drug application filing with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and into the first half of 2029.
Werewolf shareholders will own roughly 6.8% of the combined entity, while Ambros stockholders will hold about 71.7% and private placement investors approximately 21.5%. The transaction implies a valuation of about $500 million for Ambros and $47.5 million for Werewolf before the financing. The companies expect to close the deal by the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder approvals and customary conditions.
Shares of Werewolf surged more than 127% in premarket trading on the news, building on a 5.35% gain the prior session. Trading volume ballooned to roughly 94 million shares, compared with a three-month daily average of about 1.22 million. Despite the rally, the stock remained down about 32% year-to-date and 67% over the past 12 months.
A Last-Ditch Search for a Lifeline
Werewolf began hunting for strategic alternatives in February after its cash runway dwindled to less than a year. The Watertown, Massachusetts-based biotech had raised $56 million in seed financing, a $72 million Series B, and a $120 million initial public offering in 2021, but rising costs and limited near-term catalysts left the company scrambling.
As part of its effort to preserve capital, Werewolf sold assets to Jazz Pharmaceuticals and Merck KGaA (MKKGY, MKGAF). In a separate transaction disclosed in an Aug. 20 regulatory filing, Werewolf entered into an asset purchase agreement with EMD Serono Research & Development Institute, a unit of Merck KGaA, on Aug. 14. EMD agreed to pay $28 million upfront and another $5 million after technology transfer is completed for Werewolf's preclinical INDUCER platform and certain INDUKINE assets. Werewolf retained rights to continue developing its WTX-124 and WTX-330 clinical programs, with EMD granting an exclusive license to certain transferred patents supporting those programs.
Neridronate and the CRPS-1 Opportunity
Ambros is developing neridronate, an aminobisphosphonate, for complex regional pain syndrome type 1 (CRPS-1), a chronic condition formerly known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy that causes persistent, debilitating pain typically in an arm or leg following an injury. The condition affects an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 people newly diagnosed each year in the U.S., and no FDA-approved therapies currently exist.
The drug is already approved in Italy for CRPS and other indications, where it has been administered to roughly 600,000 patients. Ambros holds intellectual property rights that, combined with the FDA's Orphan Drug designation, support potential U.S. market exclusivity through 2045. The agency has also granted neridronate Breakthrough Therapy and Fast Track designations, and has indicated that positive results from a single pivotal trial could support approval.
Ambros is enrolling approximately 270 patients in the Phase 3 CRPS-RISE trial, which compares four 400 mg infusions of neridronate over 10 days against placebo, measuring the change in pain intensity from baseline to Week 12. The company is restricting enrollment to patients with the warm subtype of CRPS-1 and a positive triple-phase bone scan, a subpopulation it believes is most likely to respond to treatment. The approach draws on a 2013 Italian study that reported significant pain reduction in CRPS-1 patients receiving four 100 mg infusions of neridronate over 10 days.
The trial is expected to complete enrollment around late 2027 or early 2028, according to the federal trials register.
"We are uniquely positioned to be advancing neridronate," said Jay Hagan, CEO of Ambros Therapeutics, adding that the new funding should allow the company to reach Phase 3 results and prepare for a potential FDA filing.
Ownership Structure After the Deal
The transaction reshuffles ownership dramatically. The table below summarizes the expected equity split of the combined company before any subsequent adjustments.
Shareholder Group
Expected Ownership
Implied Value
Ambros existing stockholders
71.7%
$358.5 million
Private placement investors

$107.5 million
Werewolf stockholders
6.8%
$34.0 million
Note: Ownership percentages are based on the companies' announcements. Implied values are calculated on the $500 million pre-money valuation for Ambros and do not reflect the $150 million private placement proceeds.
The deal represents a notable reversal of fortune for Werewolf, which debuted on public markets with ambitions around its INDUKINE platform for conditionally activated cytokines. The reverse merger structure allows Ambros to access public capital markets without undertaking a traditional IPO, a path increasingly favored by private biotechs seeking funding amid a challenging financing environment.
For investors in Werewolf, the transaction offers a modest stake in a company with a clear clinical catalyst ahead. For Ambros, the Nasdaq listing and $150 million financing provide the resources to complete a registration-enabling trial in a therapeutic area with no approved treatments and a patient population desperate for relief.
The combined company's near-term focus will be executing the CRPS-RISE trial and preparing for regulatory engagement. If successful, neridronate could become the first FDA-approved therapy for CRPS-1, establishing a new standard of care in a market that has long been overlooked by major pharmaceutical companies.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
Leads Biolabs' 4-1BB Bispecific Antibody NDA Accepted, Vying to Become World's First Approved Drug Targeting This Pathway
Add to Google Preferred Sources
Nanjing Leads Biolabs (9887.HK) announced that its independently developed PD-L1/4-1BB bispecific antibody Opamtistomig has had its New Drug Application accepted by the Center for Drug Evaluation of China's National Medical Products Administration, for the treatment of advanced, previously treated extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma. The drug is the world's first 4-1BB-targeting bispecific antibody to enter NDA review and was granted priority review status in July 2026. If approved, it would become the world's first antibody drug directly targeting 4-1BB, making 4-1BB the fourth immuno-oncology target with an approved drug, following PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4, and LAG-3. The filing is based on a pivotal registrational clinical study led by Professor Shen Lin of Peking University Cancer Hospital, involving 34 hospitals and 96 enrolled patients. No approved therapy currently exists specifically for extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma worldwide, representing a significant unmet medical need. Additionally, Phase 2 data for Opamtistomig combined with chemotherapy in first-line non-small cell lung cancer showed a 65% objective response rate, with the squamous subgroup reaching 77.4%; updated data will be presented orally at the World Conference on Lung Cancer in September.
Key Elements
Leads Biolabs
Opamtistomig
China's National Medical Products Administration
Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma
4-1BB
LBL-024
Shen Lin
Peking University Cancer Hospital
U.S. Food and Drug Administration
European Medicines Agency
Nanjing Leads Biolabs Co., Ltd. (9887.HK) announced on the 21st that its independently developed PD-L1/4-1BB bispecific antibody Opamtistomig (development code LBL-024, Chinese trade name "維利信") has had its New Drug Application formally accepted by the Center for Drug Evaluation of China's National Medical Products Administration, for use as monotherapy in the treatment of previously treated advanced extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma. The application was granted priority review status on July 10, 2026. If ultimately approved, it would become the world's first antibody drug directly targeting 4-1BB, as well as the world's first approved agonist-class antibody drug.
This NDA filing is based on a pivotal registrational clinical study led by Professor Shen Lin of Peking University Cancer Hospital, with participation from 34 hospitals. The study completed enrollment of all 96 patients with extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma in August 2025, and detailed clinical data are planned for presentation at a top-tier international academic conference.
A Breakthrough in the Global Competitive Landscape
Opamtistomig is the world's first PD-L1/4-1BB bispecific antibody to enter the NDA review stage. If successfully approved, 4-1BB would become the fourth immuno-oncology therapeutic target globally with an approved drug, following PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4, and LAG-3—marking a significant breakthrough for Chinese innovative drugs in the field of tumor immunotherapy.
Leads Biolabs Chief Medical Officer Cai Xianghai stated that Opamtistomig has received multiple regulatory designations for accelerated development, including Breakthrough Therapy Designation and Priority Review status from China's Center for Drug Evaluation, Orphan Drug Designation and Fast Track designation from the U.S. FDA, and Orphan Drug Designation from the European Union.
"As the world's first 4-1BB-targeting bispecific antibody to enter registrational clinical development, Opamtistomig represents a major breakthrough in the treatment of extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma. This is a highly aggressive, immunologically 'cold' tumor for which no approved treatment regimen currently exists worldwide," said Cai Xianghai.
Company founder, Chairman, and CEO Kang Xiaoqiang noted: "Opamtistomig has the potential to become the world's first approved 4-1BB-targeting drug. This achievement reflects our 14-year commitment to differentiated innovation and our determination to conquer the most challenging targets in oncology."
The Clinical Dilemma of Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma
Neuroendocrine carcinoma is a highly malignant, immunologically "cold" tumor, accounting for approximately 10% to 20% of neuroendocrine neoplasms, and can arise in multiple organs including the lung, gastrointestinal tract, and bladder. Extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma shares similar highly aggressive and metastatic characteristics with small cell lung cancer, with rapid disease progression; most patients are already at an advanced stage or have distant metastases at diagnosis.
Currently, no regulatory agency worldwide has approved any drug specifically for the treatment of extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma. First-line treatment for advanced patients is primarily platinum-based chemotherapy, with an objective response rate of approximately 30% to 50% and a median overall survival of only about one year. After progression on first-line therapy, there is no standard treatment regimen, with second-line objective response rates of only approximately 10% to 25% and a median overall survival of about eight months.
Treatment Stage

Note: Data sourced from Leads Biolabs company announcements, reflecting the current standard-of-care landscape for extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma.
Dual-Target Mechanism and Broad-Spectrum Potential
Opamtistomig was developed using Leads Biolabs' proprietary X-body bispecific platform, capable of simultaneously blocking PD-1/L1 immunosuppressive signaling and conditionally activating the 4-1BB co-stimulatory receptor pathway, achieving a synergistic anti-tumor immune effect of "releasing the brakes while stepping on the accelerator." Its safety profile is comparable to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, but with broader anti-cancer potential.
Mechanistically, 4-1BB agonism can reinvigorate exhausted T cells and promote their robust proliferation, offering significant therapeutic promise for tumors resistant to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors or immunologically "cold" tumors, with the potential to deliver durable "long-tail" survival benefits.
To date, Opamtistomig has been studied in 13 solid tumor indications in China, including 1 pivotal registrational clinical trial and 8 proof-of-concept studies, covering extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, small cell lung cancer, biliary tract cancer, ovarian cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, triple-negative breast cancer, and malignant melanoma.
Notably, just one day before the NDA acceptance announcement, Leads Biolabs also announced that the Phase 2 clinical study abstract for Opamtistomig combined with chemotherapy in first-line non-small cell lung cancer had been accepted by the World Conference on Lung Cancer. Data showed that among 60 efficacy-evaluable patients, the objective response rate reached 65.0% with a disease control rate of 95.0%; the squamous non-small cell lung cancer subgroup achieved an even higher objective response rate of 77.4%. Updated data will be presented as an oral presentation at the World Conference on Lung Cancer on September 14, 2026.
Founded in 2012, Leads Biolabs is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing innovative therapies in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and other areas. The company has 14 differentiated drug candidates in its pipeline, including 5 clinical-stage candidates and 1 registrational-stage asset. In addition to the X-body platform, the company has established multiple proprietary technology platforms including LeadsBody (CD3 T-cell engager platform), TOPiKinectics (ADC platform), and ImBiTDC (TDC platform).

Centre imposes strict curbs on sale of four nerve-relaxing drugs
Move follows expert concerns over potential misuse and intoxication; retailers will have to maintain detailed sales records for the four CNS medicines under Schedule H1
Representative Image
Sanket Koul
New Delhi
2 min read
Last Updated :
Aug 21 2026 | 9:52 PM
IST
Listen to This Article
India’s apex drug regulator has tightened controls on the sale of four popular central nervous system (CNS) medications after expert bodies expressed concerns over their potential abuse for intoxication.
In a gazette notification released on Friday, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare inserted medications such as Flupentixol (for schizophrenia), Zopiclone (for insomnia), Gabapentin (nerve pain reliever) and Carisoprodol (muscle relaxant) into Schedule H1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.
Drugs listed under Schedule H1 require retailers and pharmacists to keep detailed records of their sales, such as the patient’s details, the name and address of the prescribing doctor, and the quantity of the drug supplied.
According to the rules, these records must be preserved for three years and made available for inspection by authorities.
The notification dated August 19 will be finalised after the completion of a 30-day period, until which stakeholders can give their feedback on the move.
Also Read

The step comes five months after the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) of the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) first recommended the inclusion of these four drugs in Schedule H1.
The recommendation was based on a report submitted by an expert committee constituted to examine proposals for listing certain drugs under Schedule H1 and Schedule X of the Drugs Rules, 1945, in light of misuse and intoxication.
The CDSCO has been taking such action on neurology and CNS drugs, a therapy segment that registered sales worth Rs 17,439 crore on a moving annual turnover (MAT, or last 12 months’ revenue) basis between August 2025 and July 2026.
The drug regulator had recently put another popular CNS drug, pregabalin, in Schedule H1 after similar concerns over potential substance abuse.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: How China’s biotech boom is bringing patients faster, more affordable drugs - BioXconomy
Drugs & Therapies.content:
Brandy Fidler
,
Editor, Business Strategy
August 21, 2026
5 Min Read
Depositphotos/Olivier26
At a Glance
Chinese biotech surged from 2% to 50% of global deal flow in just five years through rapid reforms
US patients benefit from lower drug costs and faster access as Chinese firms accelerate development
Summit Therapeutics advances groundbreaking PD-1/VEGF combo originally developed by Chinese firm Akeso
A fundamental shift in the biotech ecosystem globally is rewriting that the cost and time to market equation for drug develoment, according to Appel. Fueled by fast regulation reforms, large scale in clinical trials, and lower development costs across Asia, particularly China, an increase of next-gen therapies is making its way to Western markets at unprecedented speed.
Appel explained that in just five years, China has executed one of the most dramatic transformations in pharmaceutical history. The country has surged from representing a mere 2% of global biotech deal flow to commanding 50% of the market—effectively making it a larger force in drug innovation than the US itself.
“This is a hard thing for a lot of people to grasp,” Appel said. “How do you go from being a very small amount of the market to being the majority of the market?”
Marc Appel, founder of Pacific Bridge
The answer lies in changes that have been building for decades—and they’re helping patients far beyond China.
Related:
Innovation unleashed: The role of strategic partnerships in China
Appel says this shift is actually good news for American healthcare. Instead of being a competition where one side wins and the other loses, working together is creating more drugs, lowering costs, and reducing prices for US patients.
“Patients in the US benefit in a major way,” Appel said.
“Making better versions of existing drugs has a huge amount of value because if you make a drug less toxic or longer acting, you should get better adherence, with people on drugs for more time or experiencing fewer side effects, and that has a huge impact on overall patient outcomes.”
From manufacturing hub to innovation powerhouse
China’s biotech
evolution
spans two decades, beginning in the early 2000s as a generic drug manufacturing hub with growing preclinical and clinical research capabilities. The transformation accelerated when US-trained Chinese scientists returned home over the past decade, bringing advanced drug development expertise. Combined with aggressive government support, venture capital funding, cost-effective skilled labor, and established infrastructure, these scientists created a thriving biotech ecosystem. Chinese companies initially produced drug copies, then advanced to “best-in-class” versions with improved characteristics, according to Appel.
The results are already visible in the US market, he told us. BeiGene’s Brukinsa now competes directly with Johnson & Johnson’s drug in the hematology space. Legend Biotech developed Carvykti, a CAR-T cell therapy approved in the US for multiple myeloma. Summit Therapeutics is advancing a groundbreaking PD-1/VEGF (ivonescimab) combination molecule that targets two major cancer pathways simultaneously—originally developed by Chinese company Akeso—that shows better efficacy than either of its predecessor drug types.
Related:
China biopharma boom aided by returning talent
“These are having a big impact on patients because these are leading therapeutics. These are not small market drugs,” Appel emphasized.
Looking ahead, he noted that the trend will only accelerate. “You look five years out from now, and a large percentage of the new drugs coming on the market will have originated in China.”
Speed and cost advantage
China’s competitive edge stems from two key factors: speed and cost. The country’s large population provides access to significantly more patients than the US, enabling faster clinical trial recruitment. With fewer existing lines of therapy as standard of care, drugs can reach patients more quickly, he stated.
“You have that many more people with a particular disease,” Appel said. “As a result of that speed and frankly abundance, you get things done at much lower cost as well. That’s really helped to propel the industry forward and turn them into a major hub for biotech innovation.”
This efficiency doesn’t just benefit Chinese patients—it creates a win-win scenario for the global healthcare system. “Speeding up drug development and lowering the cost means more drugs getting to patients,” Appel explained.
Related:
China’s clinical trial reforms create new opportunities for global CROs and drugmakers
A two-way street
The collaboration between Chinese and US biotech takes multiple forms. Chinese companies frequently out-license molecules to large US pharmaceutical companies or venture capital firms that build new companies around them. On the other hand, Western companies increasingly partner with Chinese firms to run clinical trials, leveraging faster recruitment and lower costs.
“There’s capabilities that the US has, there’s capabilities China has,” Appel said.
“Working together just means we’re able to help more patients globally. Everybody sort of wins from that collaboration.”
Pacific Bridge itself exemplifies this bridging role, investing in Asian biotech assets for Western development while also helping Western companies accelerate their studies in Asia.
The regulatory evolution
A critical enabler of China’s rise has been its regulatory growth, according to Appel. The country has significantly increased oversight to match global standards, implementing orphan drug acts, clear commercialization rules, and stringent safety requirements.
“If anything, there are things that the US could probably learn from the Chinese regulatory structures now,” Appel said. “The Chinese rules are global standards, but have come about much more recently, so they’re much easier to follow and almost clearer than the US rules.
“So that’s obviously very important for China. Until China had quality of clinical development that sort of matched global standards, you really couldn’t necessarily rely on data, and I think that in recent years there’s been major shifts to come up to that global standard.”
Competitive pressures
Despite the benefits, this new landscape presents challenges. Geopolitical tensions complicate cross-border collaboration, and cultural differences can create barriers for companies without local expertise.
More fundamentally, increased competition is changing the economics of drug development, Appel noted. “The world’s become much more competitive, which means you have to move much faster just to stay afloat as a drug company,” he warned. “There’s more pricing pressures if more companies can get an approval more quickly.”
For pharmaceutical companies, distributors, and pharmacy benefit managers, this shift could reshape profit centers and commercialization strategies. “More rapid drug development and more competition in these spaces means there's certainly going to be some major changes,” Appel said. “Those who figure out how to adapt to that changing landscape will be successful.”
Appel remains optimistic about continued US-China collaboration, provided geopolitical tensions don’t worsen. “China will continue to gain more capabilities and become more sophisticated in biotech development,” he said. “At the same time, I’m hopeful that the US will continue to advance new medicines and continue to be a center of innovation.”

Invisible Work of Rare Pharmacy Delivers Highly Visible Patient Outcomes
Today's guest post comes from Jay Weaver, VP, Payer Solutions at PANTHERx
®
Rare.
Jay describes the clinical and operational work that often happens behind the scenes at a Rare Pharmacy. He explains how these capabilities—including greater personalization, real-world evidence, and specialized clinical expertise—can support therapeutic success and help payers assess the value of Rare Pharmacy.
To learn more about the PANTHERx approach to Rare Pharmacy, download their guide,
Five Criteria for Payers to Evaluate a Rare-Focused Specialty Pharmacy
.
Read on for Jay's insights.
Invisible Work of Rare Pharmacy Delivers Highly Visible Patient Outcomes
By Jay Weaver, VP, Payer Solutions, PANTHERx Rare
Rare disease therapies are among the most clinically complex and expensive treatments in healthcare. The difficult and often hidden clinical and operational work performed by a Rare Pharmacy is what helps patients and prescribers realize the full value of these therapies, including saving, improving, and extending lives. Yet much of that value remains invisible when viewed through a traditional specialty pharmacy (SP) lens.
For example, rare therapies don’t fit neatly into the evaluation and management frameworks that PBMs developed over time. Utilization management, evidence review, and cost containment strategies were built for chronic conditions, often with multiple approved therapies and large patient populations, to enable predictable forecasting. These same strategies do not always translate to rare and ultra-rare conditions.
Reshaping the value conversation
Just as the science to treat rare diseases evolves, so must our understanding of the economics. Here are three considerations for payers, PBMs, and employer groups as they assess the value of Rare Pharmacy:
1.
High personalization can uncover hidden value.
Patient education, counseling, and support continue long after the package lands on the patient’s doorstep, often at a level of intensity and duration not required in traditional SPs. Rare Pharmacy delivers an ongoing clinical relationship that involves repeated patient touchpoints, coordination with prescribers, treatment education, adherence support, benefits navigation, monitoring, and interventions when challenges arise. Much of this work occurs behind the scenes, but it is often the difference between a therapy that is prescribed and a therapy that succeeds.
2.
Rare treatments are expensive, more so if they don’t work.
A single approved rare therapy can consume an entire benefit-year budget or exceed a self-funded employer's stop-loss threshold (eg, individual injectable drug claims already reaching seven figures). In this environment, therapeutic benefit matters. Rare Pharmacy helps maximize the likelihood of success through specialized clinical support, proactive interventions, and ongoing patient engagement.
3.
Hyper-personalized treatment can reduce downstream costs.
Payers appropriately focus on matching treatments to the patients most likely to benefit,
but that approach often overlooks a
broader reality: medical utilization, disability, caregiver burden, and lost productivity frequently account for more of the
total disease cost than the drug itself. And because many rare diseases carry outsized clinical consequences for missed or delayed doses, identifying the right patient—and keeping them on therapy—matters more than in other therapeutic categories.
Patients who remain adherent to life-changing therapies are more likely to avoid complications, preserve function, reduce unnecessary healthcare utilization, and realize the outcomes that justified treatment in the first place.
Five ways Rare Pharmacy bridges payer gaps
A Rare Pharmacy like PANTHERx Rare—built specifically around rare patients rather than general specialty drug management—can address these considerations in ways most payers cannot replicate internally, through:
1.
Disease-specific clinical expertise
Clinical teams dedicated to rare conditions and treatments develop a deep understanding of disease progression and caregiver burden, enabling earlier interventions that help prevent discontinuation and avoidable complications.
2.
Real-world evidence generation
Longitudinal patient registries and outcomes tracking supplement clinical trial data, giving payers evidence of total cost-of-care offsets—not just acquisition cost—to justify continued coverage decisions.
3.
Patient identification and care coordination
A rare-focused pharmacy helps confirm appropriate therapy candidates and coordinate directly with the case managers whom payers have assigned to high-cost claimants, reducing inappropriate use and supporting confident dispensing decisions.
4.
High-touch adherence and clinical management
Tailored programs that track adherence and outcomes help demonstrate that high cost can generate high value, while close prescriber relationships ensure swift coordination when treatment concerns arise.
5.
Specialized accreditation, operations, and quality oversight
Exclusive and limited distribution capabilities, cold chain logistics, and risk evaluation and mitigation strategy program management reduce dispensing risk, while dual accreditation (eg,
URAC
and
ACHC
) and third-party quality reviews give payers confidence in the appropriateness of treatment and a reliable signal for network inclusion decisions.
Value of Rare Pharmacy extends before dispensing and after delivery
Since many rare therapies are high cost, it is in all stakeholders’ interest to ensure that a therapy is dispensed to the appropriate patients who are then counseled, closely monitored, and supported collaboratively to increase therapeutic success.
In theory, it sounds straightforward, but in practice, Rare Pharmacy is hard.
Many rare journeys involve cold chain and other precision logistics, intricate titration schedules, safety monitoring, regular laboratory assessments, and frequent patient, prescriber, and insurer touchpoints. That complexity requires more clinical interventions, coordination, expertise, and patient engagement than traditional SP models. But the reward for that additional effort is substantial: improved adherence, stronger persistence, better patient experiences, and more successful therapeutic outcomes.
My hope is that this post sparks a new conversation about how rare patients and therapies require a pharmacy model as unique as they are.

Ascendis Pharma (ASND): Three New Drugs Are Turning This Biotech Into A Growth Machine
Maham Fatima
Sat, 22 August 2026 at 6:46 am GMT+9
4 min read
ASND
On August 13, Ascendis Pharma (NASDAQ:
ASND
) reported second-quarter results that showed how far its rare disease portfolio has come. Total product revenue roughly doubled from a year earlier to €315 million, and for the first time all three of the company's approved TransCon therapies, SKYTROFA, YORVIPATH and YUVIWEL, were contributing meaningful sales in the same quarter. That combination is what management is leaning on to justify its 2030 revenue ambitions.
Ascendis Pharma (ASND): Three New Drugs Are Turning This Biotech Into A Growth Machine
Bull Case: A Portfolio Finally Firing Together
YORVIPATH, the hypoparathyroidism treatment, generated €252 million in the quarter and crossed blockbuster level on an annualized basis just two years after its U.S. launch, while reaching patients in more than 35 countries through either commercial sales or named patient access programs. Long-term trial data presented during the quarter showed response rates sustained between 82% and 86% on the combined endpoint, with patients still on therapy at a 95% rate five years after starting.
SKYTROFA, the once-weekly growth hormone therapy, crossed 20,000 unique patient enrollments and remains the best-selling long-acting growth hormone in the US as measured by brand value, contributing €55 million for the quarter. YUVIWEL, the newest of the three, launched commercially in the US during the quarter and brought in €8 million in its first quarter on the market. Enrollment kept climbing after the quarter closed, from more than 170 unique patients through June 30 to more than 220 by the end of July, with more than 65% of those patients already approved for reimbursement. Ascendis also ended the quarter with €812 million in cash and carries no bank debt or convertible debt, giving it room to keep funding these launches without outside financing.
Bear Case: The Costs Behind The Growth
The growth came with a steeper cost base. SG&A expenses rose to €173 million in the quarter from €145 million in the prior quarter, and R&D expenses climbed to €76 million from €59 million, a comparison made sharper by the fact that the prior quarter's figure had been reduced by a one-time €11 million reversal of earlier inventory write-downs. Reported operating profit of €220 million also leaned heavily on a one-time item, a €158 million gain tied to the sale of a PRV. Strip that out and non-IFRS operating profit was €92 million, a 27% margin that better reflects the underlying business. Total revenue of €339 million for the quarter also included €24 million of non-product collaboration revenue, including a €17 million milestone payment tied to TransCon CNP, money that will not repeat every quarter. And while YUVIWEL's early numbers are strong, formal regulatory decisions for the drug in the U.S. and European Union are not expected until the fourth quarter of 2026, meaning current sales are happening ahead of full approval.
Story continues
What Wall Street Is Weighing
Hedge fund ownership of Ascendis fell to 46 funds in the most recent quarter from 60 in the prior one, even as the business posted record product revenue. Short interest sits at 6.15% of the float, a level that points to a real but not overwhelming bear camp. The stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 15.92, as of August 21, a multiple that does not look priced for the growth rate YORVIPATH and YUVIWEL are currently putting up.
Where The Story Goes Next
Ascendis has moved from a single product story to a three-drug portfolio within a few quarters, and the second-quarter numbers back up management's confidence in reaching €5 billion in revenue by 2030. The bull case rests on YORVIPATH's durability data and YUVIWEL's fast start turning into sustained volume once formal approvals land later this year. The bear case rests on whether spending keeps outpacing the underlying profit line, and whether one-time gains like this quarter's voucher sale keep showing up to flatter the headline numbers.

Antibiotic resistance threatens modern medicine as bacteria evolve against life-saving drugs, demanding responsible antibiotic use, stronger research, rapid diagnostics, prevention, and coordinated global action.

Speak to Analyst
Antibiotic resistance threatens modern medicine as bacteria evolve against life-saving drugs, demanding responsible antibiotic use, stronger research, rapid diagnostics, prevention, and coordinated global action.
Modern medicine has been revolutionized by the development of antibiotics that have made deadly bacterial diseases curable. It is important for the continued efficacy of these drugs that there should be a combined effort by the government, doctors, researchers, farmers, manufacturers of drugs, and the general public. This is going to be decisive in determining whether future generations can continue to use these invaluable drugs. The rising levels of bacterial resistance to the commonly used antibiotics, and even those which had once proved very useful in treating bacterial infections, are indicative of the speed with which microbes adapt themselves to the presence of these medicines. It is true that medicines developed over the last century, which have saved countless people from death, are becoming ineffective against specific strains of bacteria. Antibiotics are good natural drugs, but microbes keep evolving in response to these medicines and develop resistance mechanisms that threaten the drugs which have changed medicine throughout the twentieth century.
Global AMR Health Statistics
Global antibiotic resistance market size is
estimated at
USD 8.9 billion in 2025
, projected to reach
USD 16.55 billion by 2035
, representing a
6.4% CAGR
from 2026-2035.
About
1 in 6
laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections associated with common infections were resistant to antibiotics in 2023.
WHO analysed more than
0.023 billion
bacteriologically confirmed cases in its 2025 surveillance report.
Resistance increased in more than
40%
of monitored pathogen-antibiotic combinations between 2018 and 2023.
Those combinations recorded average annual increases in resistance of approximately
5%-15%.
Bacterial AMR was associated with more than
4.7 million
deaths globally in 2021, according to WHO's July 2026 fact sheet.
Major Causes of Antibiotic Resistance
The growing threat of antibiotic resistance is driven by several interconnected factors, including inappropriate antibiotic use, excessive consumption in agriculture, weak infection-control practices, and limited investment in new antimicrobial treatments.
Overuse and Inappropriate Prescribing
One of the primary contributors to antibiotic resistance is the unnecessary use of antibiotics. These medicines are designed to treat bacterial infections and do not work against viral illnesses such as the common cold or influenza. However, inappropriate prescriptions, self-medication, incorrect dosages, and failure to follow treatment instructions can expose bacteria to antibiotics unnecessarily. This creates conditions in which resistant bacteria can survive, multiply, and spread.
Antibiotic Use in Livestock
Another essential factor that contributes to antimicrobial pressure is agriculture. In this industry, antibiotics are sometimes used for the treatment of infections, prevention of disease or even in order to ensure production. The wide use of antibiotics in livestock will contribute to the emergence of resistant bacteria that might later be transferred to humans through food, direct contact, agricultural waste, soil or water.
Weak Antibiotic Development Pipeline
The ineffectiveness of existing drugs calls for innovations, but the creation of new antibiotics is very complicated, time-consuming and costly. Also, there is an important issue of the commercial success of such antibiotics. The fact is that when a new antibiotic is launched, it is usually prescribed only for infections caused by resistant bacteria to slow down the emergence of resistance. This measure is essential from the medical point of view, but it can decrease the financial gains of the developer. For all such reasons, the pipeline of antibiotics has not been very strong. In 2014-2024, about 18 new antibiotics have been approved.

How Drug Resistance Is Threatening Global Health

for a personalized consultation.
Areas at Risk
The problem of antibiotic resistance makes treating common diseases such as pneumonia, urinary tract infections and sepsis much more difficult. Resistant bacteria levels vary in different countries, hence posing more problems for poor regions where there is no other medicine besides antibiotics and healthcare infrastructure. AMR is dangerous for modern medicine because surgical operations, chemotherapy, organ transplants, and care for neonates depend on antibiotics to prevent or cure infections. The more resistance occurs, the more complications arise, people remain longer in hospitals and die of their infections. Another important aspect of the problem is its economic cost. Infections that are resistant to treatment require costly interventions, tests and intensive care. In addition, resistant bacteria can circulate across countries through international travel, trade, migration, animals and food products.
Emerging Strategies to Combat Antimicrobial Resistance
Phage Therapy
Bacteriophage therapy is emerging as a potential alternative or complement to conventional antibiotics. Phages are viruses that naturally infect and destroy specific types of bacteria, allowing them to target harmful microorganisms while potentially causing less disruption to beneficial bacteria in the microbiome. Research into this approach is expanding, with clinical studies investigating its effectiveness against difficult-to-treat bacterial infections. A 2024
Nature Microbiology
study involving
100
patients reported clinical improvement in
77%
of participants, while bacterial eradication was observed in
61%
of cases in the observational study. Phage therapy continues to be evaluated through clinical research worldwide.
Artificial Intelligence Is Accelerating Antibiotic Discovery
The creation of new antibiotics often involves numerous years of research in labs, testing and financial investments. Nowadays, artificial intelligence opens new opportunities for accelerating certain stages of the process. Machine-learning models can analyse vast sets of data about chemistry and biology to find molecules with possible antibacterial properties. Moreover, the use of generative AI to design novel compounds that have the potential to be effective against microorganisms is now under consideration.
Vaccines and Microbiome-Based Approaches
The prevention of antibiotic resistance is now gaining increasing importance in the fight against it. Scientists are now working on vaccines that will protect against bacterial infections, such as those caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae. In parallel with this work, developments in the field of microbiome contribute to understanding the role that good bacteria play in protecting people from the development of infections caused by pathogenic bacteria.
Policy, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
The problem of antibiotic resistance cannot be solved solely through technological development. Effective antimicrobial stewardship programs should be put in place to ensure that antibiotics are prescribed to people who really need them. Diagnostic tests that enable doctors to differentiate between bacterial and viral diseases, thus selecting appropriate treatment, as well as the surveillance of resistance patterns and identification of emerging threats, are also necessary. The efforts made by international organisations in the area of combating antimicrobial resistance are aimed at reducing the health burden of AMR around the world.
Regional Development
Antibiotic resistance is developing differently across regions because countries vary in healthcare infrastructure, antibiotic consumption, laboratory capacity, pharmaceutical production and public-health funding. Governments and international health agencies are increasingly responding through surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, research and One Health programmes. In May 2026, the World Health Assembly adopted the updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2026–2036, providing a framework for coordinated action across human, animal, food and environmental health.
North America
The North American continent still holds significance in terms of antibiotic research, diagnostics, and healthcare innovations. Both the USA and Canada have taken initiatives in the field of antimicrobial surveillance, infection control programs, antibiotic stewardship and research. The pharmaceutical and biotechnological industry within North America provides support for developing new antibiotics, rapid diagnostics, and alternative therapies.
Europe
One of the more coordinated strategies to address AMR issues was developed by Europe, which takes into account human health, veterinary medicine and the environment. The One Health strategy used by the European Union concentrates on surveillance, infection prevention, prudent use of antimicrobials, public awareness and research. In 2023, the EU issued the Council Recommendation that included measures to fight AMR and increased commitment to national action plans, monitoring of antimicrobial consumption, infection prevention, antimicrobial stewardship and innovation.
Asia-Pacific
Asia-Pacific has become one of the focuses of global AMR efforts due to its large population, diverse healthcare systems, as well as differing levels of access to and consumption of antibiotics. In May 2024, 30 countries and areas of Asia and Pacific region endorsed a joint statement in order to speed up the process of dealing with AMR in human health. This program was initiated by Japan and facilitated by WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific regions.
Latin America
The Latin American nations are working towards strengthening AMR surveillance and proper infection prevention and antimicrobial use practices. The regional health authorities have become increasingly interested in improving the laboratory capabilities and monitoring resistance patterns, while national governments are working on implementing AMR action plans.
Africa and the Middle East
African region faces an especially tough problem with AMR due to the co-existence of resistant infections and poor access to healthcare, laboratories, surveillance and effective drugs. According to WHO, Sub-Saharan Africa has some of the highest AMR-associated mortality rates in the world. African CDC has developed regional strategies for AMR management which focus on surveillance, laboratory capacity building, antimicrobial use, infection prevention and better national policies. The strategy being developed for 2026-2030 focuses on financing, surveillance, stewardship and a One Health approach.
Challenges & Restraints
The antibiotic resistance problem faces a number of major obstacles that include the improper and excessive use of antibiotics, lack of development of new drugs, and inadequate diagnostic facilities. The development of new antibiotics is costly and takes much time since new antibiotics are usually used only for serious infections. There could be delays in the detection of resistant pathogens due to poor healthcare facilities and the lack of laboratory facilities, especially in developing countries. Ineffective infection prevention practices, wrong prescription of antibiotics, self-medicating, and the use of antimicrobials in agriculture add to the increase in the pace of antibiotic resistance. Moreover, the rapid translocation of resistant pathogens across borders complicates its control.

Uterine Fibroid Drugs Market Size & Growth Analysis
The global uterine fibroid drugs
market size was valued at USD 2.34 billion  and is projected to grow from USD 2.57 billion in 2026 to USD 5.41 billion by 2034, registering a CAGR of 9.77% during the forecast period 2026–2034. North America dominated the uterine fibroid drugs market

share of 43.18% in 2025.
Uterine fibroid drugs include gonadotropin releasing hormone agonists, GnRH antagonists, selective progesterone receptor modulators, NSAIDs, and other supportive medications. They help to improve quality of life, making them an important treatment option for women with minimally invasive management.
The uterine fibroid drugs market demand is increasing due to the rising prevalence of uterine fibroids, growing awareness of early diagnosis, and increasing preference for non-surgical treatment options. Continuous advancements in hormonal therapies, favorable reimbursement policies in developed countries, and ongoing clinical research are further supporting uterine fibroid drugs market growth.

Uterine Fibroid Drugs Market Trends
Increasing Adoption of Oral GnRH Antagonist Therapies
The market is shifting from injectable hormonal therapies toward convenient oral GnRH antagonist treatments that offer effective symptom control with improved patient adherence. This transition is driven by the growing preference for non-invasive, long-term medical management before considering surgery. As a result, pharmaceutical companies are expanding oral treatment portfolios and improving patient accessibility. For example, MYFEMBREE (relugolix combination therapy) by Myovant Sciences and Pfizer has gained significant adoption for managing heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine fibroids.
Growing Preference for Fertility Preserving Non-Surgical Treatment
Women are increasingly opting for drug-based therapies that control fibroid symptoms while preserving fertility and avoiding invasive procedures. This shift is supported by rising awareness, earlier diagnosis, and advances in targeted hormonal therapies that delay or reduce the need for surgery. Consequently, demand for innovative pharmaceutical treatments continues to expand across reproductive-age women.

Impact of Supply Chain Disruption on Uterine Fibroid Drugs Market
The Uterine Fibroid Drugs Market is indirectly exposed to supply chain disruptions due to its reliance on active pharmaceutical ingredients, specialized excipients, contract manufacturing organizations, and global pharmaceutical distribution networks. Disruptions in raw material sourcing, manufacturing operations, and international logistics can delay drug production, limit product availability, and increase procurement costs, affecting both branded and generic therapies across multiple regions. The market is demonstrating a capacity-constrained recovery, supported by stabilized API supplies, expanded production capabilities, and continued investments in supply chain resilience and pharmaceutical manufacturing infrastructure.
Uterine Fibroid Drugs Market Dynamics
Market Drivers
Increasing Clinical Adoption of Combination Therapies and Rising Adoption of Patient-specific Hormonal Treatment Drives Market
The development of combination therapies that balance symptom control with improved safety profiles is driving demand for advanced uterine fibroid drugs. These treatments help manage heavy menstrual bleeding, reduce anemia-related complications, and delay invasive procedures such as myomectomy or hysterectomy. As physicians increasingly prioritize medical management before surgery, adoption of pharmacological therapies is increasing across gynecology practices.
The shift toward personalized treatment strategies based on fibroid severity, symptom burden, and reproductive goals is increasing demand for targeted uterine fibroid drugs. Physicians are increasingly selecting therapies with adjustable dosing and improved tolerability to address diverse patient needs, particularly among women seeking to preserve fertility. For example, relugolix combination therapies provide clinicians with an option to manage moderate-to-severe fibroid symptoms while considering long-term treatment requirements.
Market Restraints
Side Effects and Competition from Minimally Invasive Procedures Restrain Market Expansion
Hormonal therapies used for uterine fibroid management can cause adverse effects such as hot flashes, bone mineral density reduction, and hormonal imbalances, limiting long-term treatment use. For example, GnRH agonists such as leuprolide acetate are generally recommended for short-term use due to risks of bone mineral density loss with extended therapy. These safety concerns require monitoring and may influence physician decisions, creating a restraint on prolonged adoption of hormonal fibroid treatments.
Advancements in minimally invasive procedures, including uterine artery embolization (UAE) and magnetic resonance guided focused ultrasound surgery, provide effective alternatives for managing symptomatic uterine fibroids without prolonged drug use. These procedures can offer faster symptom improvement and reduce dependence on continuous hormonal therapies.
Market Opportunities
Expansion of Fertility-focused Fibroid Drug Therapies and Development of Novel Non-Hormonal & Targeted Fibroid Therapies Offer Growth Opportunities
The growing focus on fertility preservation creates an opportunity for pharmaceutical companies developing uterine fibroid therapies that control symptoms while delaying or avoiding invasive procedures. This opportunity is particularly relevant for companies investing in hormonal therapies with improved safety profiles for younger women seeking pregnancy options. Future market growth is expected as personalized treatment approaches and fertility-preserving care pathways become more common. Companies such as Myovant Sciences, Pfizer, and Theramex are expanding their women’s health portfolios around advanced hormonal treatments for symptomatic fibroids.
The demand for safer long-term treatment options creates growth opportunities for drug developers working on targeted and non-hormonal approaches that overcome limitations of existing hormonal therapies. This opportunity is driving research into therapies that directly address fibroid growth pathways while reducing adverse effects. Future adoption is expected to increase as clinical validation supports broader use of innovative treatments.
Market Challenges
Complex Disease Variability and Limited Patient Identification Challenges Market Growth
The heterogeneous nature of uterine fibroids, with differences in size, location, number, and biological characteristics, creates challenges in developing therapies with consistent outcomes across patients. For example, treatments such as GnRH-based therapies may effectively reduce heavy menstrual bleeding but show variable effects on fibroid size reduction among different patients. This variability increases clinical trial complexity, requires patient-specific evaluation, and slows the development of broadly effective uterine fibroid drugs.
Another key challenge for the uterine fibroid drugs market is the delayed identification of eligible patients due to asymptomatic cases, underdiagnosis, and limited screening practices. Many women seek treatment only after symptoms become severe, reducing opportunities for early pharmacological intervention. For example, women with mild fibroid symptoms may remain untreated until heavy menstrual bleeding or anemia develops, limiting the addressable patient pool for drug therapies.

Rare disease drug Tavneos recalled in Republic of Ireland
15 hours ago
Share

A drug used to treat rare autoimmune diseases has been recalled from shelves in the Republic of Ireland.
Tavneos (Avacopan) is made by the US biotech firm Amgen and is sold by various partner pharmaceutical companies around the world.
In May, Kissei, which owns the rights to the drug in Japan, reported 20 deaths from more than 8,500 patients who had been treated with it in the country since 2022.
It is not clear if Tavneos was the direct cause of the deaths and Amgen has
previously said
"these figures include cases for which a causal relationship with the product could not be determined".
Tavneos is used to treat adults with severe and rare autoimmune diseases which cause inflammation of the blood vessels.
In July, the European Medicines Agency recommended that the drug be stripped of its market authorisation.
The European Commission endorsed that recommendation earlier this month.
The drug stopped being distributed from wholesalers in the Republic of Ireland on 11 August and the recall of any remaining stock at wholesale level was requested by the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) on Thursday.
Irish broadcaster RTÉ reports that before the European Medicines Agency's recommendation, about 60 people were treated with Tavneos.
The HPRA said the drug was only prescribed by consultants with "specialist experience in management of these conditions", and added that some had already made the decision to take patients off this drug.
The HPRA said patients currently taking the drug should not stop treatment without first consulting with their doctors.
France's medicine safety agency ANSM said the "recall of all batches" of the drug available in the country would begin on 19 August.
The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in the UK said in June that it
was reviewing
the benefits and risks of the drug.
It said it will be "communicating the outcome of our review, including any decision on its licencing status, in due course".
It added that no new patients should be started on the drug while the review is taking place.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: A New Personalized Cancer Vaccine Could Keep Skin Cancer From Coming Back, Drugmakers Say - Smithsonian Magazine
Drugs & Therapies.content:
The trial only included people with melanoma, but experts say the same treatment approach could potentially be applied more broadly—to other types of cancer, as well as rare conditions caused by genetic mutations.
LordHenriVoton / Getty Images
A personalized cancer vaccine, used in combination with an existing treatment, helped prevent the return and spread of melanoma in a late-stage clinical trial, Moderna and Merck, the companies developing the drug,
announced
this week. The results bring the vaccine, called intismeran, one step closer to regulatory approval and potentially wider use.
“This is a new chapter in cancer care,” Stéphane Bancel, chief executive officer of Moderna, tells
CNN
’s Meg Tirrell and Jamie Gumbrecht.
Intismeran is a personalized cancer vaccine, also known as an individualized neoantigen therapy. The vaccine isn’t designed to stop cancer from occurring in the first place. Rather, it aims to keep the disease from returning in patients who have already had it. It relies on the same mRNA, or messenger RNA, technology as many
Covid-19 vaccines
and a new
mRNA flu shot
. While those vaccines target viruses, intismeran uses a similar approach to fight cancer.
Did you know? The mRNA flu shot
MFlusiva, an
mRNA flu vaccine
developed by Moderna, will be available for this year's flu season for people ages 50 and up.
For this trial, a version of intismeran was created exclusively for each patient, a process that took about six weeks. Researchers made each personalized treatment by sampling the patient’s cancer tumor, then genetically sequencing the cells to identify unique mutations. Because of these mutations, tumor cells produce proteins called neoantigens, which sit on the cells’ surface. Once injected, the personalized vaccine helps train the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells that carry these neoantigens.
Researchers recruited 1,137 patients whose advanced melanoma had been surgically removed but was considered likely to return. All participants received pembrolizumab, an immunotherapy cancer treatment drug also made by Moderna and Merck and sold under the brand name Keytruda. In addition to pembrolizumab, about half of the patients were also given intismeran; the other half were given a placebo. Neither the participants nor their doctors knew who received the cancer vaccine.
According to Merck and Moderna, participants who were given both intismeran and pembrolizumab lived longer without their cancer coming back than those who only took pembrolizumab. Similarly, patients who took both intismeran and pembrolizumab went longer without developing new lesions outside the original site of the cancer.
The drugmakers did not release detailed trial data but described the results as “clinically meaningful” in a
statement
. They say they plan to present the findings at an upcoming international medical meeting and share them with regulatory authorities.
Earlier this year, Moderna and Merck shared the results of a midstage trial of intismeran and pembrolizumab. The combination of the drugs, they said, reduced the risk of melanoma’s recurrence or spread by 49 percent after five years compared to pembrolizumab alone.
Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, responsible for an
estimated
8,510 deaths per year in the United States. If detected early, melanoma is highly treatable, and most patients have a good chance of surviving. However, advanced melanoma can be difficult to treat, as it has often spread deeper into the skin or to other parts of the body.
Outside experts are awaiting the data. However, they say the results seem promising and align with the findings of other small studies conducted in recent years.
“This is really an important achievement,”
Jedd Wolchok
, the director of the Meyer Cancer Center at Weill Cornell Medicine, who was not involved with the trial, tells
STAT
’s Matthew Herper and Angus Chen. “It tells us what might have been considered science fiction 15 or 20 years ago—that we can produce a personalized vaccine based on sequencing from a tumor from a pathology specimen—could be used to delay progression of melanoma. It really establishes personalized cancer vaccines as being a new addition to standard cancer therapy.”
The trial only included people with melanoma, but experts say the results suggest the same treatment approach could potentially be applied more broadly—to other types of cancer, as well as rare conditions caused by genetic mutations, per
Nature
’s Rachel Fieldhouse and Mohana Basu.
Personalized mRNA vaccines are being developed for pancreatic, stomach, kidney, bladder, colon and lung cancers.
“We should be hearing results from multiple studies over the next few years and there’s every reason to hope now, with this news, that ​many of them will be positive,”
Robert Vonderheide
, director of Penn Medicine's Abramson Cancer Center and president-elect of the American Association for Cancer Research, tells
Reuters
’ Julie Steenhuysen.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: South Korea eases drug rules, speeds trials and strengthens GMP standards - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
Pharma Industry.content:
The Ministery of Food and Drug Safety will ease regulations so that for minor changes, such as changes in the location of pharmaceutical manufacturers and importers due to administrative district reorganizations, companies can simply file a report without going through existing approval or notification procedures.
The Ministery of Food and Drug Safety said on the 21st that it gave advance notice of legislation for a revision to the Rules on the Safety of Drugs, etc., and will accept opinions through Oct. 21.
Key points include: ▲ switching to reporting for minor changes such as location changes due to administrative district reorganizations ▲ shortening the processing period for clinical trial plan approvals ▲ shortening the submission deadline for drug recall plans ▲ international harmonization of good manufacturing practice (GMP) for investigational drugs.
First, for changes such as location changes due to administrative district reorganizations affecting pharmaceutical manufacturing, import, and contract manufacturing and sales businesses, as well as clinical trial plans, clinical trial sample analysis institutions, and nonclinical testing institutions, procedures will be simplified so that companies need only report within one year instead of obtaining change approval, notification, authorization, or designation.
Approval for clinical trial plans (and amendments) will also be improved so that, if the preliminary review results are appropriate, the statutory processing period can be shortened. This is part of the “60 tasks for food and drug safety assurance,” prepared to ease inconveniences in daily life and support the growth of new industries such as AI and biotech.
If safety or efficacy issues arise with drugs in distribution, requiring a recall, the submission deadline for the recall plan will be shortened from the current five days to three days. The measure is intended to respond quickly to recalls and enhance the safety of products in distribution.
Good manufacturing practice (GMP) standards that must be followed when making investigational drugs will also be revised to meet international standards. The changes of the Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S), which sets international good manufacturing practice standards for drugs, will be reflected.
The Ministery of Food and Drug Safety said it expects the revision to lay the groundwork for easing the regulatory burden on the pharmaceutical industry while strengthening drug quality and safety management.

Introduction
The global pharmaceutical industry is considered one of the most valuable and most fragmented major industries in the world economy. According to Precedence Research, the pharmaceutical market has reached $1.77 trillion in 2025 and is anticipated to nearly double to $3.20 trillion by 2035, yet even the industry's single largest firm, Eli Lilly, controls less than 4% of that total.
This report combines Precedence Research's market-sizing and segmentation data with each major firm's own FY2024 financial disclosures to answer, in detail, which pharmaceutical firms actually hold the largest global market share, alongside how that share is distributed across regions, disease categories, and even drug types, and what recent M&A activity along with the GLP-1 obesity-drug boom are doing to reshape the industry's competitive leaderboard in real time.
Key Takeaways
The pharmaceutical market worldwide was valued at $1.77 trillion in 2025 and is anticipated to reach $3.20 trillion by 2035, rising at a CAGR of 6.10%.
The top 12 pharmaceutical firms by revenue together control nearly 39% of the estimated $1.7 trillion 2024 global pharmaceutical market, a highly concentrated but not monopolistic industry structure.
Merck & Co.'s Keytruda is considered the world's best-selling drug in 2024 at $29.5 billion in sales, thus growing 18% and now accounting for roughly 46% of Merck's total revenue.
Eli Lilly became the world's largest pharmaceutical firm by revenue in FY2024 with $65.2 billion, overtaking longtime leaders for the strength of its GLP-1 obesity or diabetes franchise.
North America holds the largest regional share of the worldwide pharmaceutical market at 42% in 2025, while Asia Pacific is anticipated to be the fastest-growing region through 2035.
The U.S. pharmaceutical market alone was valued at $520.38 billion in 2025 and is estimated to reach $963.52 billion by 2035, approximately 29% of the entire global pharmaceutical market on its own.
Prescription medicines dominate the worldwide market with an 87% revenue share in 2025; meanwhile, conventional small-molecule drugs (55%) still edge out biologics and biosimilars (45%), though biologics are growing faster.
GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and obesity, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic or Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro or Zepbound, have become one of the fastest-growing franchises in pharmaceutical history, thus collectively approaching $50-55 billion in annual sales by 2024-2025.
Cancer is the single-largest disease category in worldwide pharmaceutical spending, generating an estimated 19% revenue share in 2025, ahead of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
Major 2024-2025 M&A activity, including AbbVie's $8.7B ImmunoGen acquisition and Novo Holdings' $16.5B Catalent acquisition, alongside J&J's $14.6B Intra-Cellular Therapies deal, shows the industry consolidating around oncology, obesity, and even manufacturing capacity.

Global Pharmaceutical Market Set to Nearly Double by 2035
According to Precedence Research, the worldwide
pharmaceutical market
starts at a baseline of USD 1.77 trillion in 2025, and it expands to USD 3.20 trillion by 2035. Thus, this trajectory reflects a steady compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.10% from 2026 through 2035, propelled by an aging demographic as well as greater
adoption of biologics
.
Key Insight
: A 6.10% compound annual growth rate sustained over a decade is a significant trajectory for a trillion-dollar-plus industry; it states the market will add more absolute value in the upcoming ten years, which is $1.43 trillion than the entire pharmaceutical market globally was worth as recently as the early 2010s.
Source: Precedence Research - "Pharmaceutical Market Size, Share and Trends 2026 to 2035 (Report Code 6227)," Updated June 23, 2026.
